title: Why I Built Luazi
content:
Luazi started as a frustration with existing scripting languages on Roblox. I wanted something with:

- Type safety without the bloat
- Memory safety that doesn't kill performance
- Multi-target compilation (WASM, C++, C#)
- A syntax that feels like Lua but with modern features

The result is a Hindley-Milner type system, ownership/borrowing inspired by Rust, and a bytecode VM that can target multiple runtimes.

```lz
fn fib(n: number) -> number {
    guard n >= 0 else { return 0 }
    match n {
        0 => 0,
        1 => 1,
        _ => fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
    }
}
```

More on the compiler architecture soon.

title: Roblox Optimization Tips That Actually Work
content:
Here are optimization techniques I use on every project, pulled from both production experience and community research:

**1. Object Pooling**
Don't Destroy() and Instance.new() in loops. Pool your parts, UI elements, and sounds. The GC pressure alone will tank your frame rate.

```luau
local pool = ObjectPool.new("Part", 100)
local part = pool:Acquire()
-- use part
pool:Release(part)
```

**2. Batch RemoteEvents**
Instead of firing 50 individual remotes per frame, batch them into a single table send. Network replication is expensive — treat it like a scarce resource.

**3. Avoid TweenService for complex sequences**
TweenService creates a new tween object every call and doesn't give you fine-grained control. A custom interpolation module with RunService.Heartbeat gives you cancellation, chaining, and zero-allocation updates.

**4. Collision Fidelity**
For objects the player can't walk on, set CollisionFidelity to Box. For complex shapes with many triangles, use Hull instead of PreciseConvexDecomposition.

**5. Mesh RenderFidelity**
Set mesh RenderFidelity to Performance for anything that isn't a hero asset. The visual difference is usually negligible, but the render cost drop is significant.

**6. Avoid Transparent and Unanchored Parts**
Semi-transparent parts and unanchored physics sims are frame-rate killers. Anchor everything that doesn't need physics, and keep transparency to a minimum.

**7. Instancing and Meshes for Repeats**
Chairs, trees, streetlights — if you repeat it, make it a Mesh or Union. The engine instanciates these far cheaper than unique Part assemblies.

**8. StreamingEnabled**
Turn it on. If your scripts break because of WaitForChild timing, fix the scripts. Streaming is one of the highest-impact optimizations you can enable.

**9. CastShadow on Micro-Details**
Grass blades, pebbles, tiny interior props — turn CastShadow off. Shadow calculation on irrelevant geometry is pure waste.

**10. Disable CanTouch and CanQuery**
Background scenery, walls, map borders — if it doesn't need hit detection, turn both off. Stops the physics engine from burning CPU on useless collision checks.

**11. Luau Compiler Directives**
Use `--!strict` for type safety, `--!optimize 2` for published games, and `--!native` for math-heavy hot paths. Native compilation translates Luau to machine-readable C++ at runtime — unbeatable speed, but higher memory footprint.

**12. Texture Discipline**
Keep textures small, reuse them aggressively, avoid semi-transparent textures, and minimize how many are active at once. Fewer active textures = less memory pressure and faster draw calls.

**13. Skip Custom Culling**
Roblox's engine-level C++ culling is faster than anything you can write in Luau. Don't fight the engine — let it handle visibility.

**14. Profile Before You Optimize**
Use the MicroProfiler to diagnose actual lag spikes. Don't guess. Measure, find the bottleneck, then fix it.

title: GitHub Learning Lecture
content:
A curated guide to learning Git and GitHub, from first commit to confident collaboration.

## Why GitHub?

Version control isn't optional once you're building anything bigger than a single script. GitHub is the industry standard for hosting, collaborating, and shipping code. Whether you're working on Roblox games, systems tools like Luazi, or open-source contributions, GitHub is the backbone.

## Core Concepts

- **Repository (repo):** A project's folder tracked by Git. Contains all files and full history.
- **Commit:** A snapshot of changes with a message describing what changed and why.
- **Branch:** An independent line of development. `main` (or `master`) is the default.
- **Pull Request (PR):** A proposal to merge changes from one branch into another. This is where code review happens.
- **Clone, Fork, Merge:** Clone copies a repo locally. Fork creates your own copy on GitHub. Merge brings branches together.

## Essential Commands

```bash
# Setup
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

# Daily workflow
git init                          # Start a new repo
git clone <url>                   # Copy a repo locally
git add <file>                    # Stage changes
git commit -m "message"           # Save a snapshot
git push origin main              # Upload to GitHub
git pull origin main              # Download latest changes
git branch feature-x              # Create a branch
git switch feature-x              # Move to that branch
git merge feature-x               # Merge branch into current
```

## Recommended Learning Path

**Phase 1 — Hello World (1–2 hours)**
- Walk through [GitHub's Hello World tutorial](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/hello-world)
- Complete [GitHub Skills: Introduction to GitHub](https://skills.github.com/)

**Phase 2 — Branching & Merging (2–3 hours)**
- Practice with [Learn Git Branching](https://learngitbranching.js.org/)
- Create branches, open pull requests, and resolve merge conflicts in a test repo

**Phase 3 — Real Collaboration**
- Fork an open-source repo and submit a PR fixing a `good first issue`
- Set up [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com/) to host a personal site or project docs

**Phase 4 — Advanced Workflows**
- Learn [GitHub Actions](https://github.com/features/actions) for CI/CD
- Explore rebasing, cherry-picking, and stashing with [Pro Git](https://git-scm.com/book)

## Best Resources

| Resource | Type | Best For |
|----------|------|----------|
| [GitHub Skills](https://skills.github.com/) | Interactive courses | Hands-on practice in real repos |
| [Learn Git Branching](https://learngitbranching.js.org/) | Visual game | Understanding branching visually |
| [Inter-Git](https://inter-git.com) | Browser tutorial | Running real commands with feedback |
| [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/) | Official docs | Reference and deep dives |
| [Pro Git](https://git-scm.com/book) | Free book | Understanding Git internals |
| [freeCodeCamp Crash Course](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RGOj5yH8evw) | Video | ~1 hour guided walkthrough |

## Pro Tips

- **Commit often, push regularly.** Small, focused commits are easier to review and revert.
- **Write meaningful commit messages.** "Fix collision bug in player controller" beats "fix stuff."
- **Use `.gitignore`.** Never commit build artifacts, secrets, or large binary files.
- **Read PRs before merging.** Even on solo projects, self-review catches bugs.
- **Don't fear the command line.** GUIs are fine, but knowing the CLI makes you unstuck when things break.

> *"The core commands you'll use daily are just a handful — `add`, `commit`, `push`, `pull`, `branch`, and `switch`. You don't need to memorize everything upfront."*

Start small. Make a repo, break something, fix it, and push. That's how you learn.
